idiom_name: axum-extra PrivateCookieJar / SignedCookieJar over the cookie crate, with a serde-encoded payload
implementation_notes: The cookie crate implements the cryptography and axum-extra wires it into extractors: CookieJar for plain cookies, SignedCookieJar for a public HMAC signature (tamper-evident, still readable) and PrivateCookieJar for values encrypted with a Key (suitable for private data); cookies are added by returning the modified jar in the response and read back with jar.get(name), and the typed session payload is yours - serialize it with serde or keep a token crate. The Key must come from application state through a FromRef implementation and be identical across instances and restarts, because Key::generate() per boot invalidates every cookie; rotation has no built-in support, so old keys must be kept and tried on decryption. A JWT crate is the interoperable alternative when other stacks must read the token; the sealed-jar form stays justified when the cookie is the carrier and the payload must remain opaque.
pitfalls: Mutating the jar without returning it from the handler drops the Set-Cookie header silently - the extractor's documented trap.
A Key generated at startup differs per process and per restart, so cookies fail to decrypt; the cookie crate ships no rotation helper, so previous keys must be retained for reads.
The encrypted, base64-encoded value is larger than the plaintext (roughly a third more) and still subject to the ~4 KB browser cookie limit.
A cookie that fails to authenticate or decrypt is simply absent from the jar, so tampering looks like an anonymous visitor unless the failure is logged.
